unit.title: Comply with regulatory and taxation requirements

summary: This unit teaches you the legal and tax duties of a small salon or spa in Jamaica: choosing and registering a business, getting a TRN, registering for and charging GCT, deducting PAYE income tax, NIS, NHT and Education Tax from staff pay and paying them over, keeping records and receipts, following health, fire, consumer, employment and privacy rules, and staying up to date. Rates and thresholds change, so you learn where to check them.

blocks.p: Every business in Jamaica must follow the law, and a salon is no exception. A salon owner has to register her business, collect and pay certain taxes, pay her staff correctly, keep proper records, keep the premises safe and clean, and protect clients' personal information. Doing these things is called **compliance**.

This unit is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees who may one day run their own salon or work in one as an employee or a self-employed stylist. You do not have to become an accountant. You do have to know **what the duties are, who deals with them, and where to check the current rules**, because rates, thresholds and due dates change.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Sole trader, partnership or limited company
Register the name or the company at the Companies Office of Jamaica
A TRN from Tax Administration Jamaica (TAJ)
A NIS number for each worker
Register when taxable sales pass the threshold; charge it; file returns; pay it over
Deduct PAYE income tax, NIS, NHT and Education Tax; add the employer's share; pay it all to TAJ; give payslips
Profit; the return; employed and self-employed stylists
Cash book, receipts, invoices, bank records, payroll records; a separate business bank account
Public health, fire safety, consumer rules, employment rules, client privacy
Compliance calendar; penalties; no tax evasion; correct mistakes quickly

flow: Register the business
Get the TRN and tax numbers
Charge and record every sale
Keep receipts and records
Run payroll and pay deductions over
File returns by their due dates
Check the rules regularly

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks. In the practicals you make a start-up compliance checklist and a 12-month calendar for a made-up salon, then keep a week's records and prepare payslips and a payroll summary from figures the assessor gives you. **Do not state a tax rate or threshold you have not checked.** Write 'check the current rules with Tax Administration Jamaica' instead.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: This kit gives no tax rates or thresholds on purpose. They change, often in the national budget. The figures in the worked examples are made up for practice only.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Type
Who owns it
Main features
rows: Simplest and cheapest. The owner and the business are the same in law, so the owner is personally responsible for the business's debts.
Two or more people who share the work and profit
Partners share profits and, usually, responsibility for debts. A written partnership agreement avoids disputes.
The company is legally separate from its owners. Owners' personal risk is normally limited, but there is more paperwork and cost.

ul: A sole trader or partnership that trades under a **business name** registers that name at the **Companies Office of Jamaica**. A limited company is formed (incorporated) there.
Registration makes the name official, tells the public who owns the business, and is required by law.
The owner also needs to know about any other approval or licence the salon needs, for example from the local municipal corporation or public health department. Ask the offices concerned.
Keep the registration documents safe. Banks, suppliers and landlords often ask to see them.

blocks.note: Registering a business does not register it for tax. Tax registration is a separate step with Tax Administration Jamaica.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Office
What it does for a salon
rows: Issues the TRN; registers for GCT and as an employer; receives returns and payments (income tax, GCT, PAYE, NIS, NHT and Education Tax); issues the Tax Compliance Certificate.
Ministry of Labour and Social Security
Employment rules, the national minimum wage and NIS.
Gives fire safety advice and inspections.
Deals with consumer rights and complaints.

blocks.note: Offices change their names, rules and forms. Always check with the office, or with an accountant or tax adviser, for the current steps.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: TRN, income tax and who pays what

ul: A **TRN** (taxpayer registration number) is issued by **TAJ**. Every person who pays or collects tax needs one: the owner, the business if it is a company, and each employee.

It is linked to your tax records. Keep it private and give it only to people who have a real need for it, such as an employer, a bank or TAJ. Someone who knows your TRN and other details could misuse it.
A NIS number comes from the National Insurance Scheme, not TAJ. An employer needs both from each new employee.

blocks.p: A business pays income tax on its **profit**, not on everything it takes in.

flow: Total income from sales
Subtract allowed business costs
The result is profit
Tax is worked out on the profit
Return filed and tax paid by the due date

ul: **Income** is all the money the business takes in from sales, before any costs are taken off.
**Expenses** are the costs of running the business: rent, electricity, stock, equipment and wages. Only costs that are for the business and that you can prove are allowed.
Example (made-up figures): income J$600,000 − allowed costs J$410,000 = profit J$190,000.
Personal costs, such as the owner's own groceries, are not business costs.

blocks.note: Keep receipts for every business cost. If TAJ asks, you must be able to prove it. A cost without a receipt may be disallowed, and then the profit and the tax rise.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: A **tax return** is a form that reports income and the tax owed. It is filed with TAJ by a **due date**.
Income tax is worked out for a 12-month **tax year**. Check TAJ for the current dates.
Even in a year with little income, a required return must still be filed.

head: Feature
Employed stylist
Self-employed stylist (for example, rents a chair)
rows: Needs a TRN and a NIS number; gives them to her employer
Needs her own TRN and registers with TAJ
Employer deducts PAYE from each pay
She files her own return and pays tax on her profit, with any advance payments TAJ requires
Employer deducts and pays them over
She pays her own contributions as TAJ requires
The employer keeps payroll records; she keeps her payslips
She keeps all sales, costs (chair rent, products, tools) and receipts
Register only if her own taxable sales pass the threshold

blocks.note: Example (made-up): a self-employed stylist takes in J$780,000 in a year. Her costs are chair rent J$312,000, products J$156,000 and tools J$24,000, a total of J$492,000. Profit = 780,000 − 492,000 = J$288,000.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **GCT** (General Consumption Tax) is a tax on the sale of many goods and services in Jamaica. A business that is registered for GCT collects it from customers on behalf of the government and pays it over.

ul: A business must register for GCT when its **taxable sales pass the threshold** set by law over a stated period. Below it, registration is not required.
The threshold and the rate can change. Check the current figures with TAJ, and watch your sales so that you register in time.
A salon should keep a running total of its sales so that it knows when it is getting near the threshold.
Charge GCT at the **current rate** on taxable services and products, and show it on receipts or tax invoices.
The GCT collected is **not the salon's money**. It belongs to the government. Keep it apart from spending money so that it is there when it is due.
File a **GCT return** by every due date TAJ sets, even in a month with few or no sales, and pay over what is owed.
The salon can usually claim back the GCT it paid on business purchases (called an **input credit**) if it holds a valid **tax invoice** from a registered supplier.

blocks.p: Simple picture (made-up figures): GCT collected from clients J$18,000 − GCT paid on stock and other purchases J$7,500 = J$10,500 to pay to TAJ.

ul: Supplier's name, address and TRN
Invoice number and date
What was sold, the quantity and the price
The GCT charged, shown separately
A scrap of paper or a note with only a total is not enough to claim an input credit.

blocks.note: A GCT-registered salon that does not file returns on time, or that spends the GCT it collected, is in breach of the law and may have to pay penalties and interest.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Employing staff: payroll and the statutory deductions

blocks.p: An employer must **deduct** certain amounts from each worker's pay, add her own share where the law requires it, and **pay everything over to TAJ**. These are called **statutory deductions** because the law requires them.

head: Deduction
What it is
What it gives the worker
rows: PAYE (Pay As You Earn) income tax
Income tax taken from wages each payday when pay is above the tax-free level.
It pays her income tax as she earns, so she does not owe a large sum at the end of the year.
A contribution by the worker and the employer.
Benefits such as a pension in later life, and help after an injury at work.
A contribution by the worker and the employer.
Access to housing loans, and a refund of contributions in certain cases.
A contribution by the worker and the employer.
Helps pay for education in Jamaica.

blocks.note: The employer must check the **current rates and thresholds** with TAJ every time they change. Never use a figure from memory.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Get each worker's TRN and NIS number
Register as an employer with TAJ
Work out gross pay
Work out each deduction at the current rates
Pay the worker her net pay and give a payslip
Add the employer's own share
Pay all of it over to TAJ by the due date

ul: **Gross pay** is pay before deductions. **Net pay** is what the worker takes home: gross pay minus all deductions.
A **payslip** should show gross pay, each deduction and net pay.
The deductions are the **worker's money**, held for her. Keeping them, or using them to buy stock when cash is short, is against the law, and the worker may lose NIS and NHT credits.
There are also other payroll duties, such as the employer's own contribution to HEART/NSTA Trust where it applies. Check TAJ for the current rules.

blocks.h: Worked example (practice figures, not real rates)

head: Item
J$
rows: Employer's share: NIS 1,650 + NHT 1,800 + Education Tax 1,500
Total to pay over to TAJ (8,190 + 4,950)

blocks.note: Pay the deductions over by the due date TAJ sets. Late payment brings penalties and interest. Put the due dates in a compliance calendar.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Employers must pay at least the **national minimum wage**. It is set by law and changes from time to time. Check the current figure with the Ministry of Labour and Social Security.

head: Records
Examples
Why
rows: Daily sales of services and products; copies of receipts given to clients; card machine slips
Shows income and the GCT collected.
Supplier invoices and receipts for stock, rent, electricity, water, phone and equipment
Proves costs and the GCT paid on purchases.
Check the cash book against the bank.
Each worker's gross pay, deductions, payslips and the amounts paid over to TAJ
Copies of returns, GCT records, registration documents

ul: Give a **receipt for every sale**, including cash sales, and record every sale in the cash book. Never leave cash sales out.
Write up the **cash book** daily or weekly. A cash book is the book (or computer file) in which money received and money paid out are recorded day by day.
Open a **separate business bank account**. Do not mix the owner's own money and the salon's money. It keeps the business figures clear and easier to track.
File receipts by month in labelled folders, or scan them and back up the files.
Keep records for as long as TAJ requires (several years). Check how long with TAJ.
Store records safely so they are not lost, damaged or read by unauthorised people.

blocks.p: **Reconciliation** means checking that two sets of records agree, such as the cash book and the bank statement. If they do not, find out why.

head: Cash book
J$
rows: Cash kept in the till for change

blocks.p: The two agree. If the deposit slips had totalled J$117,000, the J$3,000 gap would need an explanation: a missed entry, a slip not filed, or money missing. Never ignore a gap.

ul: Differences are often due to timing (a cheque that has not yet cleared) or a simple writing error.
If you cannot explain a difference, tell the owner or the accountant at once.

blocks.note: Example: the week's costs are J$71,200. Income minus costs = 128,500 − 71,200 = J$57,300 for the week, before wages and other costs not yet counted.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Other rules a salon must follow

head: Area
What the salon does
rows: Tools cleaned then disinfected; single-use items used once; fresh towels for each client; clean water; proper waste disposal and a sharps box; the public health department may inspect.
Fire extinguishers checked; exits clear; wiring safe; chemicals stored and used as the maker says, with safety data sheets and first aid at hand.
Pay at least the minimum wage; keep a written record of pay and hours; give holidays and breaks as the law requires; provide a safe workplace.
Clear prices; no false claims about products or results; receipts; fair treatment of complaints.
Client record cards contain personal information. Under Jamaica's Data Protection Act, keep them private and secure.
Check whether the municipal corporation, the health authority or other bodies require a licence or approval for the premises or the services.

ul: Check each of these with the office concerned. Rules differ and change.
Put renewals and inspections in the compliance calendar.

blocks.note: Never promise results you cannot guarantee ('this will make your hair grow in a week'). False claims break consumer rules and lose clients' trust.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A **compliance calendar** is a plan of every tax and legal task, with its due date. Many owners pay penalties simply because they forgot a date.

flow: List every duty
Check each due date with TAJ or the accountant
Write them on a wall or phone calendar
Add reminders a week before
Tick off each one when done
Review the calendar every year

head: How often
Examples
rows: Record sales and costs; bank takings; file receipts.
Pay over payroll deductions; file payroll returns; file the GCT return and pay GCT, if registered.
File the income tax return; renew registrations or file company annual returns; renew permits and inspections.

blocks.p: Write 'as TAJ sets' and the date once you have checked it. Never guess a due date.

blocks.h: What happens if you do not comply

ul: **Penalties and interest** on late returns and late payments. A small debt can grow.
TAJ can take action to collect money owed.
Leaving sales out of the records so that you pay less tax is **tax evasion**. It is against the law and can lead to heavy penalties and legal action.
Workers may lose NIS and NHT credits if their deductions are not paid over.
Without a **Tax Compliance Certificate (TCC)**, which shows that a business is up to date with its taxes, you may not be able to get certain licences, contracts or loans.
No penalties and no stress.
A good name with clients, staff, banks and suppliers.
Clear records show the true state of the business, which helps with decisions and loans.
You can get a TCC when you need one.
If you find a mistake in a return that you have already filed, act quickly and do not hide it.
Check your figures and records. Ask your accountant for help if you need it.
Contact TAJ, explain what happened and correct it as TAJ advises.
Put in place a check so that the same mistake does not happen again.
Check **TAJ** (website, offices, notices) for tax rates, thresholds and due dates.
Check the Companies Office of Jamaica for registration, and the Ministry of Labour and Social Security for the minimum wage and staff rules.
Read the news, especially around the national budget, but check it against the official source.
Ask an accountant or tax adviser how a change affects the salon.
Business and trade groups, and the HEART/NSTA Trust, can also keep owners informed.

blocks.note: Tax pays for schools, hospitals and roads that the salon, its staff and its clients use. Being honest about tax is both the law and fair.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: I can say why a salon owner must follow tax and business laws.
I can describe a sole trader, a partnership and a limited company.
I can say where a business name or company is registered.
I can say who issues a TRN and who needs one.
I can work out profit as income minus allowed costs.
I can explain when a salon must register for GCT and what it must do afterwards.
I can say why the GCT collected must be kept apart.
I can list the four statutory deductions and say what each is for.
I can work out net pay and the amount to pay over to TAJ from figures given to me.
I can say how employed and self-employed stylists differ for tax.
I can say what records a salon must keep and how to keep them in order.
I can write up a cash book and reconcile it with the bank.
I can name the other rules a salon must follow, apart from tax.
I can set up a compliance calendar.
I can explain why tax evasion is wrong and what to do about a mistake in a return.
I can say where to check the current rules.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give a reason for each step. For example: 'I keep the GCT apart from spending money, because it belongs to the government and must be paid over on the due date.'
blocks.label: Tip

c1.title: Opening a salon in Old Harbour
c1.text: Ms. Tanesha Francis plans to open 'Crown and Curls' in Old Harbour. She will be the only owner and will not form a company. She will employ two stylists and also let a third stylist rent a chair. She expects her sales to grow quickly in the first year and does not know whether she will need to register for GCT.

c2.title: Odane's pay
c2.text: Odane is a stylist at a salon in Half-Way Tree. This month his gross pay is J$55,000. The salon's payroll sheet, with practice figures, shows: PAYE J$4,200, NIS J$1,650, NHT J$1,100 and Education Tax J$1,240 deducted from him. The employer's share is NIS J$1,650, NHT J$1,800 and Education Tax J$1,500.

c3.title: A week in the cash book
c3.text: At a salon in Mandeville, the cash book for one week shows sales of J$128,500 and costs of J$71,200. The owner keeps J$8,500 in the till for change and banks the rest. The deposit slips for the week total J$120,000.

c4.title: A chair-renting stylist in Montego Bay
c4.text: Shantel rents a chair in a Montego Bay salon and works for herself. Over the year she took in J$780,000 from clients. Her costs were chair rent J$312,000, products J$156,000, tools J$24,000. She has never filed a tax return and has no receipts for her products, only a notebook.

c5.title: Money spent on stock instead of deductions
c5.text: Mr. Dwight Palmer owns a salon in Spanish Town. For two months, cash was tight, so he paid for stock with the money he had deducted from his staff's pay for NIS, NHT and Education Tax, planning to pay TAJ later. A letter from TAJ now asks why the payments are late.

questions.q: Ms. Francis is a sole trader. What does that mean if the salon cannot pay a supplier?
o: The business is separate in law, so only the salon's money can be taken
Her two stylists must share the debt equally with her
In law she and the business are one, so she is personally responsible
TAJ pays the supplier and collects it later through her taxes
questions.why: A sole trader and the business are the same person in law, so the owner is personally responsible for its debts. A limited company is legally separate from its owners.

questions.q: Before she pays her first wages to her two employees, what must she do about payroll?
o: Register as an employer with TAJ, so she can deduct and pay over
Ask each employee to pay her own PAYE, NIS, NHT and Education Tax later
Open a second business name just for the payroll
Wait until the end of the year, and ask TAJ to work out each deduction
questions.why: An employer registers with TAJ so that she can deduct PAYE, NIS, NHT and Education Tax from each pay and pay them over, with her own share, by the due dates.

questions.q: Her sales may soon pass the GCT threshold. What is the best plan?
o: Wait until TAJ sends her a letter telling her that she must register
Register in her second year, whatever her sales turn out to be
Add GCT to her prices only when a client asks her about it
Track her taxable sales and check TAJ's current threshold
questions.why: The owner is responsible for registering in time. Watching sales and checking the current threshold with TAJ means she registers when the law requires it.

questions.q: What is Odane's net pay?
What total does the salon pay over to TAJ for Odane this month?
questions.why: The deductions taken from him (J$8,190) plus the employer's share (1,650 + 1,800 + 1,500 = J$4,950) make J$13,140.

questions.q: Which deduction has no employer's share on the payroll sheet?
o: Education Tax
NIS
NHT
PAYE
questions.why: PAYE is the worker's own income tax, taken from pay, so there is no employer's share. NIS, NHT and Education Tax each have an employer's share as well.

questions.q: Odane asks why his net pay is less than his gross pay. What is the best answer?
o: The law requires tax and contributions to be taken out first
The owner keeps the difference as the salon's profit each month
The difference pays towards the salon's rent and stock bills
It is a fee charged for making up his payslip every month
questions.why: Statutory deductions come out of gross pay and are paid over to TAJ for him. They are not the owner's money, and they do not pay the salon's costs.

questions.q: How much should the owner have banked, and does it agree with the deposit slips?
o: J$120,000, and it is J$8,500 over
J$71,200, and it agrees with the slips
J$120,000, and it agrees
J$128,500, and it is J$8,500 short
questions.why: Sales of J$128,500 less J$8,500 kept in the till leave J$120,000 to bank, which matches the slips.

questions.q: What is the difference between the week's sales and costs?
questions.why: 128,500 - 71,200 = J$57,300, before wages and other costs not yet counted.

questions.q: The slips had totalled J$117,000 instead. What should the owner do?
o: Find out why J$3,000 is missing, then ask her accountant
Ignore it, because small gaps are normal in a very busy week
Change the figures in the cash book so that they agree with the slips
Put J$3,000 from the till into the bank to make it agree
questions.why: A gap must be explained: it may be a missed entry, a timing difference or missing money. Changing the books hides the problem, and ignoring it is risky.

questions.q: What is Shantel's profit for the year?
What does Shantel need to do about her income tax?
o: Pay tax on her total takings of J$780,000, not on profit
Get a TRN, file her own return and pay tax on profit
Nothing, because the salon owner pays her tax for her
Wait until TAJ writes to her and asks for the tax due
questions.why: A self-employed person runs her own business. She files her own return and pays tax on her profit. The salon owner is not responsible for her tax.

questions.q: Which habit would best help Shantel with her costs?
o: Keep every business receipt and enter each cost in a cash book
Keep a notebook only, and throw away the receipts to save space
Count all of her personal spending as business costs as well
Work out her costs at the end of the year from memory alone
questions.why: Receipts prove business costs if TAJ asks, and a cash book keeps the figures in order. A notebook alone may not be accepted, and personal spending is not an allowed cost.

questions.q: Why was it wrong to spend the deductions on stock?
o: Stock may only be paid for from the salon's bank account
TAJ allows it if the owner pays interest at a later date
They are the workers' money, to be paid over to TAJ
They belong to the salon until the end of the tax year
questions.why: Statutory deductions are taken from workers' pay for NIS, NHT and Education Tax, and belong to TAJ and the workers. Using them for anything else is against the law.

questions.q: What is the best first step now?
o: Close the salon for a few weeks until he has the money
Contact TAJ, explain, and arrange to pay what is owed
Say nothing, and hope that TAJ forgets about the letter
Take more from his staff's pay next month to catch up
questions.why: Acting quickly and honestly gives the best chance of a fair solution. Hiding it or taking more from staff makes things worse.

questions.q: What is likely to happen to the staff because of his actions?
o: Nothing at all, since the money was the owner's all along
They will be paid twice for the same two months of work
They will have to file the salon's own returns for him
They may lose NIS and NHT credits for those months
questions.why: NIS and NHT credits depend on contributions being paid over. If they are not, the workers may lose benefits.

questions.q: Which tool would best help Mr. Palmer not to miss due dates again?
o: A note stuck on the till
A weekly talk with his staff about money
A compliance calendar with reminders
A larger bank account for the salon
questions.why: A compliance calendar lists every task and its due date, with reminders, so that nothing is forgotten.

questions.q: A supplier hands over a slip that says only 'stock J$9,000'. Why is it not enough for a GCT-registered salon?
o: GCT cannot be claimed back on stock bought for resale
It is not a valid tax invoice, so no credit can be claimed
The amount is too large to be claimed back on one single slip
Slips must be typed on a computer, not written by hand
questions.why: A valid tax invoice shows the supplier's name and TRN, the date, what was sold and the GCT charged. Without it, the input credit may be refused.

questions.q: Which task belongs in a compliance calendar as a yearly task, rather than a monthly one?
o: Paying over payroll deductions
Banking the week's takings
Filing the GCT return, if registered
Filing the income tax return
questions.why: Income tax returns are filed once a year. Payroll deductions and GCT returns usually fall due more often, and banking is a routine task. Always check the dates with TAJ.

questions.q: Which of these is an allowed business cost?
o: An invoice for colour products used in the salon
The owner's weekly grocery shopping for her home
A new school bag for the owner's own child's school
The owner's family holiday to Negril in the summer
questions.why: Costs that are for the business and can be proved, such as products used in the salon, are allowed. Personal spending is not.
